questions.prompt: Pure compounds P and Q each contain 40.0% carbon by mass. A sample contains both compounds, with no reaction between them, and carbon analysis also gives 40.0% by mass. What can be concluded about the relative masses of P and Q in the sample?
options: The sample must contain a greater mass of P than of Q.
The sample must contain a greater mass of Q than of P.
The carbon analysis alone cannot determine the relative masses of P and Q.
The sample must contain equal masses of P and Q.
questions.explanation: C is correct. If the component masses are m_P and m_Q, the carbon mass is 0.400m_P + 0.400m_Q = 0.400(m_P + m_Q). Therefore every possible mixture of these two compounds has the same 40.0% carbon result. A and B each assert an unsupported inequality; neither component contributes a different carbon fraction that could reveal its proportion. D is also unsupported: equal masses give this result, but so do unequal masses. A measurement that distinguishes the two components is needed to determine their proportions.

questions.prompt: A 10.0 g sample consists of pure NaCl mixed with sand that contains no chlorine. Elemental analysis shows that the sample contains 3.55 g of chlorine. What percentage of the original sample is NaCl by mass? Use atomic masses Na = 23.0 amu and Cl = 35.5 amu.
questions.explanation: A is correct. The molar mass of NaCl is 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol. Chlorine accounts for 35.5/58.5 = 0.6068 of the mass of pure NaCl. Because all the chlorine in the sample comes from NaCl, the mass of NaCl is 3.55 g divided by 0.6068, giving 5.85 g. The percentage of NaCl in the original sample is (5.85 g/10.0 g) × 100% = 58.5%. B is incorrect because it treats the numerical mass of chlorine, 3.55 g, as though it directly represented 35.5% of the sample. C is incorrect because 60.7% is the percentage of chlorine within pure NaCl, not the percentage of NaCl in the mixture. D is incorrect because 41.5% is the percentage of sand in the mixture. Elemental analysis can determine the purity of a sample when the composition of the desired compound and the contribution of impurities are known.

questions.prompt: An 80.0 g homogeneous aqueous solution contains 20.0% NaCl by mass. A student withdraws a representative 25.0 g portion. No water evaporates and no other material is lost. What is the NaCl mass percentage in the solution remaining in the container?
questions.explanation: D is correct. The original solution contains 0.200(80.0 g) = 16.0 g NaCl. The representative portion contains 0.200(25.0 g) = 5.00 g NaCl. The remaining solution contains 11.0 g NaCl in 55.0 g solution, so its mass percentage is (11.0/55.0)100 = 20.0%. Representative sampling removes solute and solvent in the same proportion. A incorrectly keeps all 16.0 g of salt while removing solution mass. B divides the removed salt mass by the original solution mass. C divides the remaining salt mass by the original solution mass, instead of by the remaining solution mass.

questions.prompt: A gaseous mixture contains 0.200 mol of CO and 0.200 mol of CO₂. What percentage of the total mass of the mixture is carbon? Use atomic masses C = 12.0 amu and O = 16.0 amu.
questions.explanation: B is correct. The molar masses of CO and CO₂ are 28.0 g/mol and 44.0 g/mol, respectively. The mass of CO is 0.200 mol × 28.0 g/mol = 5.60 g, and the mass of CO₂ is 0.200 mol × 44.0 g/mol = 8.80 g. The total mixture mass is 14.40 g. Each molecule of CO and CO₂ contains one carbon atom, so the total amount of carbon is 0.400 mol. The carbon mass is 0.400 mol × 12.0 g/mol = 4.80 g. Therefore, the carbon mass percentage is (4.80/14.40) × 100% = 33.3%. A is incorrect because 27.3% is the carbon mass percentage in pure CO₂, not the mixture. C is incorrect because 42.9% is the carbon mass percentage in pure CO. D is incorrect because equal mole amounts of CO and CO₂ do not imply that carbon accounts for half the total mass. The elemental composition of a mixture depends on both the chemical formulas and the relative amounts of its components.

questions.prompt: A particulate model represents two samples containing stable molecular substances A and B. Sample P contains 8 molecules of A and 4 molecules of B. Sample Q contains 4 molecules of A and 8 molecules of B. No chemical reaction occurs when A and B are combined. Which statement best describes the samples?
options: Both samples are pure compounds because each contains only two types of molecules.
Sample P has the chemical formula A₂B, while Sample Q has the chemical formula AB₂.
Both samples are mixtures of the same two substances, but their relative compositions differ.
The samples must contain different chemical elements because their numbers of A and B molecules differ.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A mixture contains two or more distinct substances whose relative proportions can vary. Sample P has an A:B molecular number ratio of 8:4, or 2:1. Sample Q has an A:B ratio of 4:8, or 1:2. Both samples contain the same two molecular substances, but their compositions differ. A is incorrect because a pure substance contains only one type of constituent particle; both samples contain two distinct types of molecules. B is incorrect because A₂B and AB₂ would represent chemical formulas describing atoms chemically combined within individual particles, whereas the model describes separate molecules of A and B. D is incorrect because changing the relative numbers of molecules does not change the chemical identities of A and B. This distinction explains why mixtures can have variable compositions while pure compounds have fixed chemical formulas.

questions.prompt: A pure compound contains 40.0% carbon by mass. A 5.00 g laboratory sample contains the compound mixed with an impurity that contains no carbon. Elemental analysis shows that the laboratory sample contains 36.0% carbon by mass. What percentage of the laboratory sample is the pure compound?
questions.explanation: A is correct. Because the impurity contains no carbon, all the carbon measured in the laboratory sample must come from the pure compound. The mass of carbon in the 5.00 g sample is 5.00 g × 0.360 = 1.80 g. Since carbon represents 40.0% of the pure compound's mass, the mass of pure compound is 1.80 g/0.400 = 4.50 g. The percentage of pure compound in the laboratory sample is (4.50 g/5.00 g) × 100% = 90.0%. Equivalently, the purity can be calculated directly as 36.0%/40.0% = 0.900. B is incorrect because 10.0% is the impurity percentage, not the purity. C is incorrect because 36.0% is the carbon percentage of the entire laboratory sample. D is incorrect because 40.0% is the carbon percentage within the pure compound. This method works because the impurity is specified to contain none of the element used in the analysis.

questions.prompt: A representative particle model of a homogeneous mixture shows equal numbers of molecules of compounds P and Q. The molar mass of P is 20.0 g/mol and that of Q is 60.0 g/mol. Which statement describes the mixture by mass?
options: Each compound accounts for 50.0% of the mass because their molecule counts are equal.
Compound Q accounts for 75.0% of the mass.
Compound P accounts for 75.0% of the mass.
The mass fractions cannot be determined without knowing the absolute number of molecules.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Equal numbers of molecules correspond to equal mole amounts, n. The component masses are 20.0n and 60.0n grams, so the mass fraction of Q is 60.0n/(20.0n + 60.0n) = 0.750. A confuses equal particle counts with equal masses; a Q molecule is three times as massive as a P molecule. C reverses the components: P contributes 25.0%, not 75.0%. D is incorrect because the common mole amount cancels in the ratio; an absolute particle count is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A gas mixture contains 2.20 g of CO₂ and 3.20 g of O₂. What percentage of the total mass of the mixture is oxygen? Use atomic masses C = 12.0 amu and O = 16.0 amu.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Oxygen is present in both components of the mixture. The molar mass of CO₂ is 44.0 g/mol, of which 32.0 g/mol comes from oxygen. Therefore, the mass of oxygen contributed by CO₂ is 2.20 g × (32.0/44.0) = 1.60 g. Because O₂ contains only oxygen, the 3.20 g of O₂ contributes another 3.20 g of oxygen. The total oxygen mass is 1.60 g + 3.20 g = 4.80 g. The total mixture mass is 2.20 g + 3.20 g = 5.40 g. The oxygen mass percentage is (4.80/5.40) × 100% = 88.9%. A is incorrect because 59.3% counts only the oxygen from O₂ and ignores the oxygen in CO₂. B is incorrect because 29.6% counts only the oxygen contributed by CO₂. C is incorrect because 40.7% is the mass percentage of CO₂ in the mixture, not the percentage of oxygen. Elemental analysis of a mixture must account for an element's contribution from every component containing that element.

questions.prompt: A dry mixture of CaCO3 and SiO2 has visibly separated into layers. A student analyzes a small sample from only the top layer and finds 50.0% CaCO3 by mass. Which evaluation of the claim that the entire container is 50.0% CaCO3 by mass is best?
options: The claim is unsupported because the top-layer sample may be unrepresentative; mixing and representative sampling are needed to estimate the bulk composition.
The claim is supported because each pure compound has a fixed composition, so their mixture must also have a fixed mixing ratio.
The result proves that half of all formula units in the entire container are CaCO3.
Repeating the same top-layer sampling many times eliminates the possible sampling bias.
questions.explanation: A is correct. A layered, heterogeneous mixture can have different component proportions in different regions. A top-layer result need not describe the bulk material. A thoroughly mixed, representative sample is needed for a defensible bulk estimate. B confuses fixed elemental proportions within a compound with the variable relative amounts of compounds in a mixture. C both extrapolates an unrepresentative sample and equates a mass fraction with a formula-unit fraction; CaCO3 and SiO2 have different formula masses. D confuses precision with representativeness: repeated sampling from the same biased location can reproduce a biased result.

questions.prompt: A pure sample of MgO contains approximately 39.7% oxygen by mass. A laboratory sample believed to contain MgO is found to contain only 30.0% oxygen by mass. Assuming the sample contains MgO mixed with exactly one of the substances listed below, which impurity could explain the lower measured oxygen percentage? Use atomic masses Mg = 24.3 amu, Si = 28.1 amu, H = 1.0 amu, and O = 16.0 amu.
options: Pure O₂, which contains 100% oxygen by mass
H₂O, which contains approximately 88.9% oxygen by mass
Mg metal, which contains 0% oxygen by mass
SiO₂, which contains approximately 53.3% oxygen by mass
questions.explanation: C is correct. A mixture's elemental mass percentage is a mass-weighted average of the elemental mass percentages of its components. Pure MgO contains approximately 16.0/(24.3 + 16.0) × 100% = 39.7% oxygen. Mixing MgO with magnesium metal, which contains no oxygen, decreases the overall oxygen percentage. A sufficiently large amount of Mg metal could reduce the oxygen percentage to 30.0%. A is incorrect because adding pure O₂, which contains 100% oxygen by mass, would increase the oxygen percentage above 39.7%. B is incorrect because water contains approximately 88.9% oxygen by mass, so adding water would also increase the oxygen percentage. D is incorrect because SiO₂ contains approximately 53.3% oxygen by mass, greater than the oxygen percentage of MgO, so adding SiO₂ would increase rather than decrease the mixture's oxygen percentage. The measured composition of a mixture must lie between the corresponding elemental mass percentages of its components.

questions.prompt: A student analyzes a homogeneous aqueous NaCl solution that is known to contain 15.0% NaCl by mass. The student places 20.0 g of the solution in an evaporating dish and heats it to remove the water. The student then measures 3.50 g of solid residue, even though the expected mass of NaCl is 3.00 g. Which experimental error would best explain the unexpectedly high measured residue mass?
options: Some NaCl was accidentally spilled from the evaporating dish before the final mass was measured.
Some water remained in the evaporating dish with the NaCl when the residue was weighed.
The original solution contained less than 15.0% NaCl by mass.
Some NaCl was lost through splattering during the heating process.
questions.explanation: B is correct. A 20.0 g sample of a solution containing 15.0% NaCl by mass should contain 20.0 g × 0.150 = 3.00 g NaCl. If the water is completely removed without losing any NaCl, the final dry residue should have a mass of 3.00 g. A measured residue mass of 3.50 g is greater than expected. If some water remained in the evaporating dish, the measured mass would include both NaCl and residual water, producing an artificially high result. A is incorrect because spilling NaCl would decrease the measured residue mass. C is incorrect because a lower initial NaCl concentration would produce less than 3.00 g of NaCl in a 20.0 g sample, not more. D is incorrect because losing NaCl through splattering would also decrease the measured residue mass. This experiment illustrates how the composition of a mixture can be determined through mass measurements and how incomplete separation can introduce systematic error.
